name: Dusty vermilion
lede: Dusty vermilion renders Terigaki (照柿), a traditional Japanese name meaning "glazed persimmon", after the shine of a ripe persimmon's skin.

sections.title: Named for a ripe fruit
sections.body:
Our color library gives the source as 照柿 (Terigaki): teri is shine or glaze, and kaki is the persimmon, so the name points to the lacquered gleam of the fruit's ripe orange-red skin [1]. No first-recorded date survives in our sources, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1].

The nearest named color in our graph is [[vermilion]] itself, at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 3.3, a more vivid shade; the related [[dusty-scarlet]] sits 5.5 away and reads lighter [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this orange-red in 126 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.5 percent, as photographed [3]. It is heavily concentrated in Indian court painting, more than fifteen times the overall rate, with Kalighat work alone running nearly forty times that average, Rajput work twenty-seven times it, and Pahari work close to thirteen times it [3]. The earliest dated match is a *Madonna and Child* by the Master of San Torpè, from 1320, a floor set by what survives and was photographed, not a first appearance; the color peaks again in the 1890s, led by Henri Matisse [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; the match is computed, not a pigment identification [3].
